note: Shows n-gram decontamination is defeated by paraphrase, and finds 8 to 18 percent HumanEval overlap in common pretraining sets.
title: Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination for Language Models with Rephrased Samples
explain_beginner: Companies building AI language models try to remove benchmark test questions from the huge piles of internet text used to train them, so the model cannot simply memorize the test answers ahead of time. This paper asks whether the standard method for doing that removal, checking for exact or near exact overlapping chunks of text, actually works. Yang and coauthors found that it does not, if a test question is only slightly reworded, or translated into another language and back, the standard checking method misses it completely, even though the model can still effectively have memorized the answer. Using a smarter, AI assisted checking method instead of simple text matching, they found that 8 to 18 percent of a well known coding test set, HumanEval, was already hidden inside two commonly used public training datasets. To show why this matters, they trained a 13 billion parameter model on data containing these disguised, reworded test questions and found it could reach performance on par with GPT-4, a far larger and more capable model, purely by having secretly seen the answers. Their fix is not perfect either, but it catches disguised contamination that older methods completely missed.
explain_business: This paper's core warning for anyone comparing AI language models on published benchmark scores is that a model's training data could contain reworded versions of the exact test questions, undetected by the standard industry decontamination method, meaning an impressively high benchmark score is not reliable proof of real capability. This directly affects vendor selection and internal model evaluation, if a procurement decision leans on a benchmark number without knowing what decontamination method the vendor used, and whether that method can catch paraphrased overlap and not just exact text matches, the score may reflect memorization rather than genuine skill. The actionable step available now is that the authors released their LLM based decontamination tool publicly, so an organization building or fine tuning its own models can check training data against target benchmarks before trusting the resulting scores, and organizations evaluating vendors can reasonably ask which decontamination method, exact match or semantic, was used to validate the numbers being presented to them.
explain_practitioner: The authors show that n-gram based decontamination, the industry standard method of stripping out training text that closely matches a benchmark's exact wording, fails against paraphrased or translated benchmark samples, because these rewordings share little literal text overlap with the original questions despite testing the identical underlying problem. They replace it with an LLM based decontamination detector, then apply it to two widely used pretraining corpora, RedPajama-Data-1T and StarCoder-Data, finding 8 to 18 percent overlap with the HumanEval coding benchmark that n-gram methods had missed entirely. Their controlled experiment is the key evidence, fine tuning a 13 billion parameter model on data containing these rephrased benchmark samples let it reach performance on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval on par with GPT-4, demonstrating that undetected contamination alone, not genuine capability gain, can produce headline grabbing benchmark numbers. They further find that even synthetic training data generated by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 themselves can unintentionally reproduce rephrased benchmark content, so contamination can enter a pipeline indirectly through model generated data, not only through scraped web text.
